newsitem.title: USA: Virginia Power seeks rate freeze, special rates.
newsitem.headline: Virginia Power seeks rate freeze, special rates.

text.p: Virginia Power said Monday it filed with the State Corporation Commission to freeze the company's base electric rates through 2002.
The utility said the filing also seeks regulatory permission to offer special rates to promote the development of existing businesses and attract new ventures to Virginia.
Legislation passed in 1996 allows utilities to offer economic development rates, subject to commission approval.
The Dominion Resources Inc subsidiary said the base rate freeze is part of an alternative regulation plan submitted Monday to the commission.
The legislation requires the commission to issue guidelines ensuring that the economic discounts will not raise rates for other customers.
As part of today's filing, Virginia Power said, it is asking the SCC to issue those guidelines.
The company said it has proposed a two-phase approach to electric utility competition and restructuring.
During the first, five-year phase, base rates would be frozen and some company earnings would be used to offset the potentially high costs associated with the transition to competition.
A portion of the earnings could also be returned to customers through refunds and to shareholders through higher earnings, Virginia Power's statement continued.
Officials were not immediately available to comment on the earnings impact of the proposal.
The utility said a second phase would begin if and when competition arrives.
The company said it is seeking approval in concept of a Transition Cost Charge which would apply to customers who elect to leave the system to cover costs stranded by their departure.

Noting that a few states have already adopted rules allowing competition in retail electric service and similar steps are being considered by Congress, the utility said both the Virginia General Assembly and state regulators are conducting studies to determine if restructuring the electric utility industry would benefit consumers in Virginia.

Virginia Power noted legislation adopted by the 1996 General Assembly allows the commission to approve alternative regulation plans for state utilities if such proposals are judged to further the public interest.

If the base rate freeze is approved, the utility said, it would give Virginia Power customers a decade of stable base rates, since the last such increase occurred in 1992. Base rates make up about 75 percent of a typical Virginia Power residential bill and cover most company costs, plus profits.

With the proposed freeze in base rates, the average residential electric bill is expected to be virtually the same in 2002 as it was in 1992. When adjusted for inflation, the average bill is expected to decrease by 20 percent or more during the ten-year period.
The utility said its proposed alternative regulation plan will not affect the company's fuel charge, a dollar-for-dollar pass-through of the utility's fuel expenses.

Fuel charges to customers have declined about 16 percent over the past five years. Even with a slight rise that is anticipated in the future, customer bills in 2002 are expected to be at 1992 levels, it said.
